# **Systematic Evaluation, Error Analysis, and Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Singer Identification on Artist20**

## **Diagnostic Error Analysis Framework for Singer Identification**

### **Acoustic Confound Disambiguation and Source Separation Precedents**

Automated singer identification (SID) systems operating on polyphonic audio mixtures encounter fundamental challenges that distinguish them from standard computer vision or generic signal classification tasks. In polyphonic music, vocal formants, pitch trajectories, and timbral characteristics are combined with instrumental accompaniment, room reverberation, and studio production chains1. Early empirical work demonstrated that classifiers trained on randomly split track distributions frequently overfit to recording environment acoustics, guitar distortion profiles, and mastering equalization rather than isolating intrinsic vocal physiology3. This structural vulnerability was formally conceptualized by Kim et al. as the "album effect," wherein classifier accuracy degrades sharply when evaluated on albums not present in the training set4.  
To prevent models from exploiting these shortcut cues, benchmark evaluations on the Artist20 dataset rely on an album-level split rule, ensuring that training, validation, and test sets contain tracks from non-overlapping albums1. The evaluation paradigm established by Hsieh et al. explicitly addresses accompaniment confounds by leveraging deep source separation tools—such as Open-Unmix—to isolate singing voice stems from background instrumentation1. Under this methodology, models are evaluated across three distinct signal states to isolate sources of error1:

> 1. **Raw Polyphonic Mixture Evaluation**: Models are tested on original mixed tracks. High error rates under this condition may stem from either vocal timbral confusion or background instrumental overlap1.  
> 2. **Isolated Vocal Stem Evaluation**: Models are evaluated on vocal stems separated via deep source separation1. A substantial reduction in misclassification compared to raw mixtures confirms that background accompaniment acted as a primary confound in the polyphonic setting2.  
> 3. **Shuffle-and-Remix Augmentation Evaluation**: Isolated vocal stems of target singers are artificially remixed with instrumental stems extracted from disparate songs and genres1. Robust performance under this condition validates that the model has learned invariant vocal representations rather than relying on contextual musical background1.

Comparing error distributions across these three evaluation conditions provides a empirical diagnostic for determining whether an artist identification system keys on authentic vocal physiology or surface-level production artifacts1.

### **Musicological Taxonomy and Five-Dimensional Confusion Checklist**

To move beyond numerical confusion matrices, pairwise inter-class errors across the 20 artist classes must be audited using an acoustically and musicologically grounded framework. Evaluators can apply a structured five-dimensional checklist to diagnose inter-class confusions across specific acoustic and production variables.

| Diagnostic Dimension | Primary Acoustic Correlates | Musicological and Production Drivers | Expected Error Vectors |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Vocal Register & Tessitura** | Fundamental Frequency (![][image1]) mean, ![][image1] variance, pitch contour trajectory8 | Operatic/contemporary voice classification (Baritone, Tenor, Contralto, Mezzo-Soprano, Soprano)10 | High confusion between singers operating in identical pitch registers (e.g., Suzanne Vega vs. Tori Amos)10. |
| **2\. Phonation & Timbral Envelope** | Formant Frequencies (![][image2]), Spectral Envelope, Spectral Tilt, Harmonic-to-Noise Ratio (HNR)8 | Phonation modes (breathy, modal, creaky/vocal fry, pressed/belted)11 | Confusion between singers exhibiting raspy, heavily belted chest voice delivery (e.g., Stevie Nicks vs. Sia)11. |
| **3\. Production & DSP Chain** | Dynamic Range, Spectral Flatness, Spectral Rolloff, High-Frequency Energy Shelf4 | Vocal chain processing (heavy dynamic compression, pitch correction, slapback delay, spatial reverb)4 | Classifiers mapping distinct singers to shared modern pop production or brickwall dynamic limiting (e.g., Madonna)2. |
| **4\. Instrumental Texture** | Accompaniment Energy Ratio, Spectral Contrast, Low-frequency energy, Harmonicity4 | Accompaniment density (sparse acoustic guitar vs. wall-of-sound electric guitars/synthesizers)8 | Confusion between different vocalists backed by heavy rock instrumentation (e.g., Metallica vs. Led Zeppelin)14. |
| **5\. Vocal Arrangement Complexity** | Multi-pitch tracking variance, Formant dispersion, Harmonic multiplicity9 | Lead solo vocal vs. multi-vocal group harmonies and double-tracked leads4 | Higher error rates in band-based acts featuring prominent backing or shared vocals (e.g., Fleetwood Mac, The Beatles)4. |

When conducting error analysis, each persistent pairwise confusion cell in the confusion matrix undergoes a four-step diagnostic audit:  
First, calculate the mean and standard deviation of the fundamental frequency (![][image1]) extracted across vocal frames for both confused artists to verify whether tessitura overlap drives the error8. Second, estimate the first two formant center frequencies (![][image3] and ![][image4]) during sustained vowel segments; proximity in ![][image5] space indicates structural similarity in vocal tract length and articulation. Third, compute the spectral tilt and harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR) to evaluate phonation mode similarity, distinguishing breathy delivery from pressed belting11. Fourth, measure non-vocal spectral energy during singing pauses to determine if background accompaniment signatures dominate the misclassification decision2.

### **Localized Feature Attribution for Hand-Crafted Classifiers**

In Task 1 classifiers (such as Support Vector Machines, ![][image6]\-Nearest Neighbors, and Random Forests), global feature importance rankings summarize overall model behavior but fail to explain why specific pairs of artists are confused14. To connect hand-crafted acoustic features—such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), Chroma, Spectral Contrast, Zero-Crossing Rate (ZCR), and Tonnetz—to specific pairwise errors, localized attribution metrics must be computed8.  
The Pairwise Feature Discriminability Index (![][image7]) quantifies how effectively a given feature ![][image8] separates the feature space between two specific confused classes, artist ![][image9] and artist ![][image10]:  
![][image11]  
Where ![][image12] and ![][image13] represent the mean and standard deviation of feature ![][image8] across all audio frames or summary vectors belonging to artist ![][image9]. A low ![][image7] score across primary MFCCs indicates that the feature representation lacks the spectral resolution needed to differentiate the timbral envelopes of those two singers8.  
For non-linear models such as Random Forests, class-specific Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) provide localized feature attributions for individual class outputs16. To explain a specific directional error where tracks from artist ![][image9] are misclassified as artist ![][image10], compute the average directional SHAP contribution:  
![][image14]  
Where ![][image15] is the subset of artist ![][image9] tracks misclassified as artist ![][image10], and ![][image16] is the SHAP value of feature ![][image8] for class ![][image17]16. If higher-order MFCCs (![][image18]) exhibit negative directional SHAP values for the true class, the misclassification is driven by inadequate vocal timbral resolution8. Conversely, if Spectral Contrast or ZCR exhibits the highest directional SHAP value for the incorrect class, the error is primarily driven by background noise floor or distortion similarities8.

### **Statistical Significance Procedures for Small Evaluation Datasets**

Evaluating models on small validation partitions (such as ![][image19] or ![][image20] tracks) introduces substantial sample variance. On a 231-track test set, a single track misclassification changes the reported top-1 accuracy by approximately ![][image21] percentage points. Consequently, performance variations of ![][image22] to ![][image23] between ensemble variants cannot be assumed to reflect true structural improvements without rigorous statistical validation18.  
To evaluate whether two classifiers exhibit statistically significant performance differences on the exact same test partition, McNemar's test is applied to their paired binary predictions18. Given a contingency table tracking agreement and disagreement between Model ![][image9] and Model ![][image10], the test statistic incorporates a continuity correction:  
![][image24]  
Where ![][image25] represents the count of tracks correctly classified by Model ![][image9] but misclassified by Model ![][image10], and ![][image26] represents the count of tracks correctly classified by Model ![][image10] but misclassified by Model ![][image9]18. A calculated ![][image27]\-value below ![][image28] rejects the null hypothesis of equal error rates, confirming a statistically meaningful performance difference18.  
To report metric stability for top-1 and top-3 accuracy, non-parametric bootstrap resampling using ![][image29] iterations serves as the standard convention in speech and music evaluation literature18. Resampling the held-out test set with replacement yields an empirical distribution from which ![][image30] percentile confidence intervals (![][image31] and ![][image32] percentiles) are extracted18. Reporting confidence intervals alongside point estimates (e.g., Top-1 Accuracy: ![][image33] \[95% CI: ![][image34]\]) prevents over-interpreting minor random accuracy fluctuations18.

## **Qualitative Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Inference on Sia's "Unstoppable"**

### **Acoustic and Vocal Profile of Sia's Performance**

Evaluating an out-of-distribution (OOD) audio sample—such as an informal Voice Memos recording of a vocalist singing along to Sia's "Unstoppable"—tests classifier behavior when forced to evaluate input outside its closed 20-artist label space. "Unstoppable" (produced by Christopher Braide for Sia's album *This Is Acting*) is an anthemic pop-soul composition characterized by high dynamic compression, prominent vocal placement, and broad spatial reverb20.  
Sia Furler's vocal performance on this track exhibits distinct physical and stylistic attributes:  
Vocal range analysis places Sia as a Lyric Mezzo-Soprano with a documented overall range spanning approximately ![][image35] to ![][image36]10. On "Unstoppable," her delivery centers in the upper-midrange tessitura, featuring sustained, powerful chest belting between ![][image37] and ![][image38]20. Phonatory characteristics include high subglottal pressure during belted passages, intentional vocal cracks at register transitions, a textured raspy timbre driven by subharmonic vocal fry, and a wide vibrato11. Modern pop production techniques further alter the signal via heavy dynamic range limiting, high-frequency equalization shelf boosts (![][image39]), and double-tracked vocal layers4.

### **Timbral and Production Attribution of Closed-Set Classifier Predictions**

When evaluating the OOD clip of "Unstoppable," different model architectures distributed softmax probabilities across distinct subset clusters:

* sota\_crnn\_wide (Top-3): Tori Amos (![][image40]), Queen (![][image41]), Fleetwood Mac (![][image42])  
* sota\_crnn: Madonna (![][image43]), Fleetwood Mac (![][image42]), Roxette (![][image44])  
* ECAPA-TDNN (Pretrained Speaker Embedding): Fleetwood Mac (![][image45]), Roxette (![][image46]), Tori Amos (![][image47])  
* confound\_crnn: Madonna (![][image48]), Radiohead (![][image49]), Prince (![][image50])

Cross-referencing these outputs against musicological literature reveals whether individual models keyed on authentic vocal similarity or surface production artifacts.

| Predicted Artist | Lead Vocalist & Register | Documented Vocal / Stylistic Parallel to Sia | Primary Attribution Driver |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Tori Amos** | Tori Amos (Mezzo-Soprano, ![][image51])10 | Shares an identical mezzo-soprano vocal classification, wide pitch range, dynamic vocal cracks, and expressive chest-to-head register shifts10. | **Vocal Physiology & Timbre**: Direct alignment in pitch register, vocal break mechanics, and expressive delivery10. |
| **Queen** | Freddie Mercury (Tenor / High Chest Belt) | Characterized by powerful upper-register chest belting, wide dynamic range, high subglottal pressure, and dramatic vocal breaks. | **Vocal Mechanics**: Alignment in high-energy chest belting and upper-midrange formant intensity. |
| **Fleetwood Mac** | Stevie Nicks (Contralto / Mezzo-Soprano) | Characterized by a distinctive raspy, gravelly timbre, vocal fry, subharmonic friction, and a textured vocal envelope11. | **Phonation & Timbre**: Direct match on vocal raspiness, subharmonic noise, and textured acoustic edge11. |
| **Roxette** | Marie Fredriksson (Mezzo-Soprano / Belt) | Features Scandinavian power-pop belting with compressed upper-midrange vocal projection and anthemic pop delivery. | **Genre & Phonation**: Alignment in anthemic pop vocal projection and compressed upper-midrange energy. |
| **Madonna** | Madonna (Light Lyric Soprano / Mezzo) | Processed pop vocal chain featuring heavy dynamic range compression, high-frequency EQ shelf boost, and polished double-tracking4. | **Production Artifact**: Overfitting to pop vocal processing, dynamic limiting, and bright EQ mastering profiles2. |

The predictions generated by sota\_crnn\_wide (Tori Amos, Queen, Fleetwood Mac) align with Sia's acoustic vocal attributes: tessitura proximity (Tori Amos)10, high chest-belt energy (Freddie Mercury / Queen), and vocal raspiness (Stevie Nicks / Fleetwood Mac)11. In contrast, earlier or less constrained models—such as confound\_crnn assigning ![][image48] probability to Madonna—exhibit reliance on production-level confounds2. Madonna's tracks in the Artist20 dataset feature polished pop mastering and dynamic compression4. Models that fail to separate vocal timbre from mastering chains tend to map any modern, heavily compressed pop vocal directly to Madonna2.

### **Generalization Behavior of Out-of-Distribution Audio Classifiers**

The observed predictions illustrate broader phenomena documented in music information retrieval and audio classification literature regarding out-of-distribution inputs12.  
When closed-set neural networks process an unlearned vocal identity, their output distributions are governed by two distinct latent mechanisms:

> 1. **Spectral Envelope Clustering (Timbral Mapping)**: Deep convolutional architectures operating on mel-spectrograms encode vocal timbre via vertical spectral energy distributions (formants) and horizontal temporal continuity (pitch contours)2. When presented with an OOD sample, a well-regularized network maps the input to the nearest cluster in its latent embedding space based on formant spacing, vocal fry, or belt intensity2. This explains why timbrally robust models select Tori Amos, Queen, and Fleetwood Mac10.  
> 2. **Macro-Statistical Acoustic Confounds (Production Shortcuts)**: Audio classifiers remain highly sensitive to overall spectral tilt, energy distribution across frequency bands, dynamic compression ratios, and room reverberation profiles4. If an architecture overfits to accompaniment or studio mastering signatures, an OOD pop track featuring heavy dynamic limiting will trigger predictions for whichever training class possesses the highest dynamic compression levels (such as Madonna or Roxette), regardless of vocal pitch or singer gender2.

Models trained on separated vocal stems demonstrate higher timbral fidelity on OOD inputs, whereas models trained on unseparated polyphonic audio remain susceptible to production-level shortcut learning1.

## **Comprehensive Diagnostic Protocols for Model Assessment**

### **Model Probability Calibration and Uncertainty Quantification**

Standard evaluation metrics such as top-1 accuracy evaluate discrete class predictions but fail to measure whether a model's output probabilities reflect true likelihoods. A well-calibrated classifier that assigns a confidence score of ![][image52] to a group of predictions should be correct in approximately ![][image53] of those instances24. Calibration analysis is essential for evaluating out-of-distribution inputs: an uncalibrated model may assign high confidence to an incorrect out-of-distribution class (e.g., confound\_crnn predicting Madonna at ![][image48]), whereas a well-calibrated model expresses uncertainty through flat probability distributions across classes (e.g., sota\_crnn\_wide distributing confidence between ![][image54] and ![][image55])24.  
To quantify probability calibration across architectures, the probability space ![][image56] is partitioned into ![][image57] equally spaced bins ![][image58]. The Expected Calibration Error (![][image59]) calculates the weighted average difference between bin accuracy and bin confidence26:  
![][image60]  
Where ![][image61] is the total sample count, ![][image62] is the empirical accuracy within bin ![][image58], and ![][image63] is the average predicted probability within bin ![][image58]26.  
Complementing ![][image59], the multi-class Brier Score (![][image64]) measures the mean squared error between predicted probability vectors ![][image65] and one-hot ground-truth vectors ![][image66]24:  
![][image67]  
Lower Brier Scores indicate superior calibration24. Applying post-hoc calibration techniques—such as Temperature Scaling, which optimizes a single scalar parameter ![][image68] on validation logits prior to softmax—can reduce ![][image59] without altering discrete classification accuracy29.

### **Per-Album Confound Diagnostics and Residual Overfitting Metrics**

Because the Artist20 dataset partitions tracks by album, evaluating per-artist accuracy across individual test albums verifies whether architectures have successfully bypassed production confounds1.  
To quantify whether an architecture has eliminated the album effect, feature representations are evaluated across separate albums belonging to the same artist4. The Cross-Album Intra-Artist Distance Ratio (![][image69]) measures the ratio of intra-artist cross-album feature distance to inter-artist feature distance:  
![][image70]  
Where ![][image71] represents the latent embedding vector extracted from the final hidden layer, and ![][image72] is the cosine distance metric. A ![][image69] score approaching ![][image73] indicates that the model clusters representations by album production rather than artist identity, signaling persistent album effect confounds4. Conversely, a low ![][image69] score (![][image74]) confirms that latent representations cluster tightly by artist identity across disparate album productions4.

### **Latent Embedding Space Geometry and Cluster Separability**

While t-SNE visualizations provide qualitative views of embedding distributions, they do not provide quantitative measurements of cluster separability30. Latent representations extracted from final hidden layers should be evaluated using formal distance geometry metrics30.  
The Intra-to-Inter Class Cosine Distance Ratio (![][image75]) evaluates the average pairwise cosine distance within the same artist class relative to the distance across different artist classes:  
![][image76]  
In parallel, the Silhouette Coefficient (![][image77]) measures individual sample embedding separation:  
![][image78]  
Where ![][image79] represents the mean intra-cluster distance of sample ![][image80], and ![][image81] represents the mean nearest-cluster distance for sample ![][image80]. Higher average Silhouette scores confirm stronger architectural generalization across unseen album splits30.

## **Strategic Summary of Analytical Recommendations**

To ensure maximum analytical depth and technical completeness, the final report should incorporate the following core components:  
First, calculate ![][image30] non-parametric bootstrap confidence intervals across all model evaluations and apply McNemar's test when asserting performance gains between candidate architectures18. Second, replace global feature importance rankings in Task 1 with Pairwise Feature Discriminability Index (![][image7]) scores and directional SHAP values to explain specific inter-class confusions16. Third, frame the Sia "Unstoppable" out-of-distribution evaluation around musicological vocal comparisons10, contrasting models that matched on vocal timbre (Tori Amos, Queen, Fleetwood Mac)10 against those that overfit to production confounds (Madonna)2. Fourth, incorporate quantitative calibration metrics (![][image59], Brier Score) and latent geometry indices (![][image69], ![][image75]) alongside summary accuracy tables to evaluate model uncertainty and confound mitigation rigorously4.
